title: GPWS Explained: Why Cockpit Warnings Save Your Life | MSFS A-Z (Letter G)
description:
At 500 feet above the ground, a synthetic robotic voice is the only thing standing between hundreds of passengers and a sheer granite mountain wall. What keeps you off the terrain isn't luck—it's complex avionics logic actively calculating closure rates, descent envelopes, and configuration traps in real time.

Welcome back to Microsoft Flight Simulator A to Z! In this episode, we arrive at the letter G for GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) and EGPWS. If you've ever had an approach interrupted by a screaming cockpit alarm or wondered why real pilots never ignore these synthetic callouts, this breakdown covers the exact logic running behind your avionics suite.

In this video, we break down real-world avionics warnings and demonstrate how they function inside Microsoft Flight Simulator. We explore dynamic descent envelopes, terrain closure rates, post-takeoff altitude drops, and why enhanced forward-looking terrain databases changed aviation safety forever.

In this video, you’ll discover:

- Mode 1 (Excessive Descent Rate): How dynamic trigger envelopes scale from 4,000 FPM down to 1,500 FPM near the ground.
- Mode 2 (Terrain Closure Rate): Why level flight into rising terrain triggers warnings before breaking cloud cover.
- Mode 3 (Altitude Loss After Takeoff): How the system guards against spatial disorientation on initial climb-out.
- Mode 4 (Unsafe Gear/Flap Configuration): How automated logic prevents accidental belly landings below 500 feet.
- The EGPWS Revolution: Why moving beyond radio altimeter "downward canes" to forward-looking GPS terrain ribbons eliminated blind spots.

Understanding your cockpit callouts and reacting correctly within 3 seconds is what separates casual flight simmers from elite virtual pilots. Next time your avionics blare a terrain warning in MSFS, respect the envelope and pull up immediately. If this systems breakdown helped sharpen your flight technique, hit that like button, subscribe for the rest of our aviation alphabet series, and let me know in the comments: what’s the closest near-miss you've ever had with terrain in MSFS?
